notes.meaning: While Saul lay immobilized under the prophetic power at Naioth, David fled back toward Gibeah to meet with Jonathan. He asked Jonathan three times what wrong or sin he had done against Saul to make the king want him dead. David knew he was completely innocent of any crime against the throne, but he also needed to find out whether Jonathan stood with him or with Saul.

Jonathan refused to believe that David was in real danger, assuring him he would not die. He reasoned that Saul shared every matter with him, whether large or small, and would never keep such a deadly plan secret. Out of love and respect for his father, Jonathan assumed Saul's past violent outbursts were temporary fits rather than a settled plot to murder David.

David confirmed his danger with a solemn oath, swearing by the living God and by Jonathan's own life. He explained that Saul knew of their close bond and had purposefully hidden his murderous designs so Jonathan would not be grieved. David warned that his peril was urgent and extreme, describing himself as being only a single step away from death.

Jonathan was moved by David's words and offered to do whatever David asked of him. He did not dismiss his friend's fears or scold him for being discouraged, but offered loyal, practical help. True friendship shows itself in a ready willingness to serve another in times of deep trouble.

David proposed a plan based on the upcoming New Moon feast, a monthly religious and civil festival where he was expected to sit at the royal table as Saul's son-in-law and military officer. Instead of attending, David asked to stay away and hide in the open field until the third evening. This planned absence would serve as a test to see how Saul would react when David failed to appear.

David instructed Jonathan that if Saul asked about his absence, he should say David urgently asked permission to travel to his hometown of Bethlehem for an annual family sacrifice. Jonathan had authority as the king's son and deputy to grant temporary leave to military leaders. This excuse provided an understandable reason for David to be away while the two friends watched the king's response.

Saul's reaction would reveal his true heart. If the king calmly accepted David's absence, it would show he held no murderous grudges and David would be safe. If Saul became furious, it would prove that his mind was firmly set on doing evil against David.

David appealed to Jonathan to act faithfully because they had entered a sacred covenant together before the Lord. A covenant is a solemn, binding promise made in the presence of God. David was so sure of his innocence that he told Jonathan to kill him on the spot if he was guilty of any crime against the king, rather than hand him over to Saul.

Jonathan strongly rejected the thought that he would ever harm David or hide danger from him. He spoke with intense emotion, insisting that if he discovered his father had decided to do evil against David, he would warn him right away. He could not bear the thought of betraying their shared trust.

David then raised a practical problem about how the warning would reach him. He asked who would bring the report if Saul responded angrily, since an enraged king would suspect Jonathan and might keep him from communicating freely. The two friends needed a safe way to deliver the message without putting either of them in further danger.

Jonathan invited David to walk out into the open country with him. Leaving the royal residence allowed them to speak privately, far from the eyes and ears of Saul's servants. Out in the quiet field, they could plan their secret signal and speak freely before God.

Jonathan called upon the Lord, the God of Israel, as his witness and began a solemn vow. He promised to test his father's intentions by that time the next day or the day after. If Saul felt kindly toward David, Jonathan swore that he would send word and let David know the good news.

Jonathan called down God's severe punishment upon himself if he failed to warn David should Saul intend to do him harm. He promised to help David escape safely so he could go in peace. In wishing that the Lord would be with David just as He had once been with Saul, Jonathan acknowledged that God was preparing David to take his father's place as king.

Looking ahead to David's future reign, Jonathan asked David to show him the Lord's faithful love throughout his lifetime so that he would not be put to death. In ancient times, new kings often killed off members of the previous royal family to remove any rivals to the throne. Jonathan trusted David to act differently by keeping God's covenant mercy toward him.

Jonathan asked David to extend this same unfailing kindness to his family and descendants forever. Even when the Lord wiped out all of David's enemies from the earth, Jonathan wanted his own household spared and cared for. This request showed Jonathan's absolute certainty that God would defeat David's foes and establish David's royal line.

Jonathan broadened his personal covenant with David into a lasting pact that bound both of their households across future generations. He called on the Lord to bring judgment against any enemies who sought David's ruin or broke this sacred promise. In later years, David remembered this solemn agreement by showing great kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth.

Jonathan had David swear to the covenant once more because of the deep love he held for him. Jonathan loved David as much as he loved his own life, and he wanted this bond of friendship to stand firm without end. A true and godly friendship puts aside selfish ambition and rejoices in God's will for others.

Jonathan returned to the practical details of their plan. He reminded David that the New Moon festival began the next day, and that his absence from the royal table would be immediately noticed because his customary seat would be empty. That empty chair would soon force Saul to reveal his true feelings about David.

Jonathan told David to wait for three days and then go down to the place where he had hidden during the earlier trouble with Saul. David was instructed to wait beside a recognizable landmark known as the stone Ezel, which was likely a trail marker near a suitable hiding spot. There David could stay hidden out of sight while waiting for Jonathan's signal.

Jonathan planned to go out into the field with his bow and shoot three arrows to the side of the stone, pretending to practice target shooting. This clever cover story would allow him to be in the area with weapons without making Saul's watchers suspicious. The arrows would serve as the hidden sign of life or death for David.

Jonathan explained the code he would use with the young boy who retrieved his arrows. If Jonathan called out to the boy that the arrows were on his near side, David would know by that sign that it was completely safe to return to court. Jonathan swore by the living Lord that this signal meant peace, with no threat or danger to David's life.
